content:
An infant in southwestern Wisconsin has died of measles — the state's first measles death in 36 years, and the third measles-related death reported in the United States this week.

The Wisconsin Department of Health Services announced the death Thursday, Nov. 5. The coroner listed measles as the infant's immediate cause of death. State officials did not release the child's age, county of residence, or other details to protect the family's privacy, though the Milwaukee Journal Sentinel reported the death was in Grant County. Grant County health officer Kessa Klaas said the infant was too young to be vaccinated.

"It is with a heavy heart we are reporting the first death of an infant connected with a measles outbreak in Wisconsin in many years," said Department of Health Services Secretary Kirsten Johnson. "My heart is broken for the family."

An outbreak at a 35-year high

Wisconsin has reported 431 measles cases in 13 counties so far in 2026 — the highest count the state has seen in more than 35 years. Nine people have been hospitalized. All but three of the cases were in people who were unvaccinated. Three southwestern counties — Lafayette with 155 cases, Grant with 142, and Iowa with 97 — account for more than 90% of the state's total. Wisconsin recorded just 36 cases in all of 2025.

State health officials cautioned that the true number is most likely higher, because not everyone who gets sick seeks medical care or gets tested.

A national toll that keeps rising

The Wisconsin death follows New York's first measles death in 30 years, reported just days earlier. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has confirmed 4,852 measles cases nationwide as of Oct. 29, including four fatal cases confirmed by the CDC, while state health departments have reported higher totals — eight deaths in 2026, including six in Pennsylvania, one in New York, and one in Wisconsin, according to state reports. At least four of the deaths involved children or infants.

Measles is a highly contagious viral disease preventable through vaccination. The MMR vaccine is normally first given at 12 to 15 months of age, which means infants younger than that depend on the immunity of the people around them. Health officials stress that community vaccination rates need to stay high to protect babies too young to be vaccinated. Texas has already seen measles deaths in 2026, as Webb Watch 956 previously reported.

Families with questions about measles or vaccination can contact their doctor or a local clinic.
